title: Fewest Power-of-Two Steps to Zero
statement:
You start with a positive integer n. In one step you may add or subtract any power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …) to the current value. Intermediate values may grow larger than n.

Return the smallest number of steps that brings the value to exactly 0.

examples.why: 15 has four 1-bits, but you do not need four steps: add 1 to get 16, then subtract 16.
5 is 101 in binary: subtract 1, then subtract 4. Adding first (5 + 1 = 6, which is 110) leaves two bits and costs one step more.
23 is 10111. Add 1 to merge the run of three 1s into a single carry (24 = 11000), then subtract 8 and 16.

hints: Look at n in binary. A lone 1-bit costs exactly one step to remove. What about a run of several 1-bits in a row?

Adding the lowest set bit turns a whole run of 1s into a single carry bit further left. Subtracting it removes just that one bit. At each point only those two moves on the lowest set bit are worth trying.
Scan from the lowest bit: if the last two bits are 11, add 1 (merge the run); if they are 01, subtract 1; if the last bit is 0, shift right. Count the add and subtract moves.

explain.intuition:
Think in binary. Each step adds or removes one power of two, so the question is how to clear all the 1-bits with as few moves as possible. A lone 1 (like the 1s in 101) is best removed directly: one step. A run of two or more 1s, like 0111, is cheaper to "round up": adding the lowest bit turns it into 1000, which is one bit, so a run of any length costs about two steps instead of its length.

That gives a greedy scan from the lowest bit. If the two lowest bits are 11, we are inside a run of at least two, so add 1 and the carry ripples up. If they are 01, the bit is alone, so subtract it. A 0 bit costs nothing: shift it away. Shifting turns "add 2k" into "add 1" at the current position, so the same rule applies to every bit.
steps: While n > 0: if n & 3 equals 3, do n += 1 and count a step.
Else if n & 1 is 1, do n -= 1 and count a step.
pitfalls: Answering with the number of 1-bits. Runs of 1s are cheaper to round up: 15 needs 2 steps, not 4.
Always rounding up. A lone 1 followed by a 0 should be subtracted; adding there creates a new carry and wastes a step, as in 5.
Thinking only of subtraction because the target is smaller. Overshooting past n and coming back down is often optimal.

solutions.title: Try both moves on the lowest bit, with memo
solutions.idea: Only the lowest set bit matters next: either subtract it or add it. Recurse on both, stopping at a power of two (one step).

solutions.title: Greedy bit scan
solutions.idea: From the lowest bit: on 11 add one to collapse the run, on 01 subtract the lone bit, on 0 shift.

followups: Return the actual sequence of powers to add and subtract, not just the count.
